title: Capt. John Strode of Strode's Station
summary: Virginia veteran John Strode raised Strode’s Station on Strode’s Creek by 1779, the largest fortified settlement in what became Clark County.
bodyMarkdown:
John Strode was one of the Virginians who came over the mountains during the Revolution. According to the [Kentucky Historical Society marker for Capt. John Strode](https://history.ky.gov/markers/capt-john-strode), he came from Virginia to Boonesborough in 1776. By 1779 he had built Strode's Station, which the marker calls "the largest and most important fortified area" in what became Clark County during the early years of settlement.

## Land that was already claimed

The country around Strode's Creek was not empty. More than [50 significant prehistoric sites](https://grokipedia.com/page/Clark_County,_Kentucky) are recorded in Clark County. In the early 1700s the Shawnee town of Eskippakithiki stood in the county, and the people used the land for hunting, corn and trade along the warrior paths.

The town was [abandoned around 1750](https://grokipedia.com/page/Clark_County,_Kentucky) amid intertribal pressures ([the story of the 1753 raid](/stories/odawa-raid-at-eskippakithiki-1753/) tells part of it). The Cherokee also contested the region's deer and bison hunting grounds.

For the Shawnee and their neighbors, Kentucky remained valuable hunting land after the towns were gone. The raids on Clark County outposts were [driven by](https://grokipedia.com/page/Clark_County,_Kentucky) settler "encroachment on shared hunting domains." Virginia land warrants and the 1775 Transylvania Purchase brought farm settlement in larger numbers and behind fortifications.

## A fort under attack

Strode's Station was one of those fortifications. The marker records that Native warriors attacked the station in 1781 and again later. Two men were killed in the first attack and none in the later ones. The marker does not name the attackers or give the dates of the later raids.

Danger was close by. In June 1780, Ruddell's Station, also in what was then Bourbon County, was [captured by British and Shawnee forces](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bourbon_County,_Kentucky) (see [Isaac Ruddell and the guns at Ruddell's Station](/stories/isaac-ruddell-and-the-guns-at-ruddells-station/)). That article names the founder of Strode's Station as "Jacob Strode." The marker gives John, and this story follows the marker.

## Where a county began

When the Kentucky General Assembly created Clark County on December 6, 1792, it directed the new county's justices to meet at the house of John Strode and "fix upon a place to hold courts," the [Winchester Sun reports](https://winchestersun.com/2023/04/29/enoch-origin-of-the-name-winchester/). The justices adjourned from Strode's house and met that same day at John Baker's house. On December 17, 1793, the legislature established the town of Winchester on Baker's land ([Winchester, Clark County seat](/stories/winchester-clark-county-seat/)).

## Kentucky today

The marker stands about a mile west of [Winchester](https://grokipedia.com/page/Winchester,_Kentucky) on US 60. The station's old burial ground was unearthed in 1965, and the remains were reinterred in Winchester Cemetery. Strode's Creek still flows through Clark County. Near Paris, the Fort Ancient villages of the [Buckner Site](/stories/buckner-site-fort-ancient-villages-on-strodes-creek/) show that farming towns stood along the creek centuries before the station.
